newsitem.title: USA: Obesity, weight gain raise women's stroke risk.
newsitem.headline: Obesity, weight gain raise women's stroke risk.

text.p: Obese women and women who gain a lot of weight as adults increased their risk of suffering the most common form of stroke, researchers said on Tuesday.

After adjusting for risk factors such as smoking, age and postmenopausal hormone use, researchers at Boston's Brigham and Women's Hospital found that extremely obese women were more than twice as likely to suffer ischemic stroke compared with lean women.

About half the 866 strokes recorded in the study were ischemic strokes, in which an artery or vessel blockage stops blood and oxygen from reaching the brain. Usually, about 80 percent of strokes are ischemic.
The researchers related a woman's body mass index, a calculation combining height and weight, to her risk of stroke.

For instance, a 5-foot-5-inch (1.65 m) woman weighing 163 pounds (74 kg), with an index of 27, increased her risk 1.7 times compared with a normal woman. A 5-foot-5 woman weighing 192 pounds (87 kg), with an index of 32, raised her risk 2.4 times.

Similarly, middle-aged women who had gained between 22 pounds (10 kg) and 44 pounds (20 kg) since age 18 were 1.7 times more likely to suffer ischemic stroke than women who had gained less than 11 pounds (5 kg). Adult weight gain of more than 44 pounds raised stroke risk more than 2-1/2 times.
The study examined data from 116,759 women aged 30 to 55 who participated in the Nurses' Health Study over 16 years, beginning in 1976.

Lead researcher Kathryn Rexrodt wrote in the Journal of the American Medical Association that the link between strokes and weight might be related to the higher incidence of diabetes, high cholesterol and elevated blood pressure among obese people.
About one-third of U.S. women are considered obese, meaning they weigh at least 20 percent more than doctors recommend.
Among the 866 strokes recorded in the study, 269 were hemorrhagic strokes, in which a ruptured blood vessel bleeds into the brain. Another 194 strokes were of unknown cause.
The researchers found no evidence that weight gain and obesity raised the risk of hemorrhagic strokes.
"Obesity -- especially in women -- continues to be a serious epidemic in this country, and now there is strong evidence of yet another health risk for overweight women," Rexrodt wrote.

"There are many things women can do to help prevent stroke, such as quitting smoking, keeping blood pressure down, treating diabetes, maintaining healthy weight, exercising and eating a balanced diet," she wrote.
